Apple has filed its opposition to OpenAI's motion to dismiss the lawsuit alleging trade secret theft against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Details below.

A bit of background

A few days ago, OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss Apple's lawsuit against the company, io Products, Chang Liu, and Tang Tan, in which Apple accused the parties of trade secret theft.

In its motion, OpenAI said Apple filed the suit "without conducting a sufficient investigation," and went on to detail its own account of the events that led to Apple's filing.

OpenAI's opposition hinged on three main arguments: that Apple "failed to identify a protectable trade secret," "failed to allege conduct that could plausibly support an infringement claim," and "failed to plausibly allege any damage or ongoing harm."

OpenAI claims that contrary to Apple's allegations, former Apple employee Chang Liu provided assistance after departing in response to inquiries from a former colleague, rather than accessing Apple's data without authorization, while former Apple VP Tang Tan retained Apple exit paperwork to ensure new employees complied with the company's security procedures.

The company also argued that Apple bore some responsibility for its own information management and offboarding processes, noting that Apple encouraged employees to use personal iCloud accounts for work and failed to properly cut off departing employees' access to company data.

"Apple's complaint identifies specific individuals stealing specific Apple trade secrets in specific ways"

Today, Apple filed its opposition to OpenAI's motion to dismiss, countering each of OpenAI's arguments and stating that "in short, Defendants sidestep the striking allegations at the core of the complaint."

Apple argued its original complaint "adequately identifies the specific trade secrets that Defendants allegedly infringed," citing prior cases in which courts had ruled that similar levels of detail were sufficient for trade secret misappropriation claims to proceed.

Apple also called OpenAI's claim that it failed to adequately protect its trade secrets "equally untenable," saying OpenAI "dismisses Apple's trade secrets as merely 'supplier relationships' and then questions whether any 'supplier relationships' qualify as confidential."

The company further argued that OpenAI was essentially abusing the motion to dismiss process. From the filing:

In its opposition, Apple also directly addressed a heavily redacted transcript of a conversation posted by OpenAI on its website. In the conversation, a former colleague still at Apple reached out to Chang Liu to clarify some information about an Apple project.

OpenAI argued that the conversation proved Apple's characterization of Liu's access to data after his departure as theft was misleading, because it was Apple's own employee who proactively sought his help to get information.
